--- title: "The Immigration Question" date: "2026-02-06" categories: [economics, immigration, ABS] image: image.png format: html: code-fold: false jupyter: python3 --- ## G'day Mates! Dinki here. Today we're tackling a big one: immigration. I've heard the chatter down at the billabong—"without new folks, the economy would go belly up!" Is it true, or just a load of old cobblers? Let's have a sqiz at the numbers. ## The Dig We're pulling straight from the ABS. No messing about. **Data Sources**: - [Australian National Accounts: National Income, Expenditure and Product](https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/economy/national-accounts/australian-national-accounts-national-income-expenditure-and-product/sep-2025) - [National, state and territory population](https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/people/population/national-state-and-territory-population/jun-2025) ::: {#cell-analysis .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Load GDP Data # 5206002_Expenditure_Volume_Measures.xlsx, Table 2 path_gdp = "../../source_data/2026-02-06-immigration-economy/5206002_Expenditure_Volume_Measures.xlsx" path_pop = "../../source_data/2026-02-06-immigration-economy/310101.xlsx" def get_abs_series(path, sheet_name, keyword): # Read metadata rows (0-9) df_meta = pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name=sheet_name, header=None, nrows=10) # search for keyword in the first few rows (usually row 0 has the description) target_col_idx = None found_desc = "" for col in df_meta.columns: # Check first row specifically as it contains the main description desc = str(df_meta.iloc[0, col]) if keyword.lower() in desc.lower(): target_col_idx = col found_desc = desc break if target_col_idx is None: # Fallback: search all rows for col in df_meta.columns: if df_meta[col].astype(str).str.contains(keyword, case=False).any(): target_col_idx = col break if target_col_idx is None: raise ValueError(f"Keyword '{keyword}' not found in {path}") print(f"Found '{keyword}' in column {target_col_idx}: {found_desc}") # Get Series ID from row 9 series_id = df_meta.iloc[9, target_col_idx] # Read full data # Header=9 means row 9 is the header (Series IDs) df = pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name=sheet_name, header=9, index_col=0, parse_dates=True) return df[series_id] # GDP: "Gross domestic product" (in Table 2 this will be the Level) gdp_series = get_abs_series(path_gdp, 'Data1', "Gross domestic product") # Population: "Estimated Resident Population (ERP) ; Australia" pop_series = get_abs_series(path_pop, 'Data1', "Estimated Resident Population (ERP) ; Australia") # Merge df = pd.DataFrame() df['Real GDP'] = gdp_series df['Population'] = pop_series # GDP is usually Quarterly, Pop is usually Quarterly. # Drop NaNs df = df.dropna() # Calculate GDP per Capita df['GDP per Capita'] = df['Real GDP'] / df['Population'] # Index to 100 for proper comparison # Let's start from a reasonable timeframe, say year 2000 if available, or just start of data start_date = '2000-01-01' if start_date in df.index: df = df.loc[start_date:] else: # If data implies earlier, just use what we have, but ensuring overlap. pass base_gdp = df['Real GDP'].iloc[0] base_capita = df['GDP per Capita'].iloc[0] df['GDP Index'] = (df['Real GDP'] / base_gdp) * 100 df['GDP per Capita Index'] = (df['GDP per Capita'] / base_capita) * 100 display(df.tail()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Found 'Gross domestic product' in column 41: GROSS DOMESTIC PRODUCT ; ``` ::: ::: ## What We Found ::: {#cell-visualization .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6)) sns.lineplot(data=df[['GDP Index', 'GDP per Capita Index']], linewidth=2.5) plt.title('Australia: Real GDP vs GDP per Capita (Index 2000 = 100)', fontsize=16) plt.ylabel('Index', fontsize=12) plt.xlabel('Year', fontsize=12) plt.legend(['Real GDP (Total Size)', 'GDP per Capita (Individual Share)']) # Add annotation for COVID plt.axvline(x=datetime(2020, 3, 1), color='red', linestyle='--', alpha=0.5) plt.text(datetime(2020, 3, 1), df['GDP Index'].max(), ' COVID-19', color='red', verticalalignment='top') plt.tight_layout() plt.show() # Quick CAGR calc start_val = df['GDP Index'].iloc[0] end_val = df['GDP Index'].iloc[-1] years = (df.index[-1] - df.index[0]).days / 365.25 cagr_gdp = (end_val / start_val)**(1/years) - 1 start_cap = df['GDP per Capita Index'].iloc[0] end_cap = df['GDP per Capita Index'].iloc[-1] cagr_cap = (end_cap / start_cap)**(1/years) - 1 print(f"Annual Growth Rate (GDP): {cagr_gdp:.2%}") print(f"Annual Growth Rate (GDP per Capita): {cagr_cap:.2%}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/visualization-output-1.png){#visualization width=1135 height=561} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Annual Growth Rate (GDP): 3.08% Annual Growth Rate (GDP per Capita): 1.66% ``` ::: ::: The blue line—Total GDP—is rocketing up. That's the "economy growing". But the orange line—your share of the pie—is growing much slower. In fact, in recent years (post-COVID), you can see the per-capita growth has flattened or even dipped, while the total GDP kept chugging along (mostly). This implies that a huge chunk of our "economic growth" is just... more people. Not necessarily more productivity or wealth per person. ## Conclusion So, would the economy collapse without immigration? Typical economist answer: "It depends what you mean by economy." If you mean **Total GDP**, then yeah, it would likely shrink or stall given our aging workforce. But if you mean **Living Standards (GDP per Capita)**, the picture is murky. The data shows we aren't getting individually richer at the same rate the country is. Immigration keeps the *aggregate* numbers looking shiny, but for the average punter, it's a bit of a slower ride.
